questions.q: State the SI unit of power and write its relationship with joule and second.
questions.a: The SI unit of power is watt (W). 1 W = 1 J/s. A wrong answer like "joule" or "newton" reveals the student confuses power with work or force. Writing "W = J × s" shows they misunderstand the rate concept as multiplication instead of division.

questions.q: Two students, A and B, each lift a 20 kg box to a height of 2 m. Student A takes 4 seconds, student B takes 8 seconds. Who has greater power? Explain why the work done is the same but power differs.
questions.a: Student A has greater power. Work done = mgh = 20 × 10 × 2 = 400 J for both. Power of A = 400/4 = 100 W; Power of B = 400/8 = 50 W. Same work, less time means higher power. A wrong answer claiming B has more power because "he took more time" reveals the misconception that power increases with time, confusing total energy with rate.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW water pump runs for 2 hours daily. Calculate the electrical energy consumed in one day in joules and in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
questions.a: Power = 1.5 kW = 1500 W. Time = 2 h = 7200 s. Energy in joules = P × t = 1500 × 7200 = 10,800,000 J = 1.08 × 10^7 J. Energy in kWh = 1.5 kW × 2 h = 3 kWh. A wrong answer of 3000 J (using kW × seconds without conversion) reveals unit inconsistency: mixing kW with seconds instead of hours for kWh, or forgetting to convert kW to W for joules.

questions.q: A graph shows work done (y-axis) versus time (x-axis) for two machines: Machine X is a straight line through origin with slope 500; Machine Y is a horizontal line at 2000 J after 2 seconds. Compare their power outputs and explain the physical meaning of the slope.
questions.a: Machine X has constant power of 500 W (slope = ΔW/Δt = power). Machine Y does 2000 J in 2 s (average power 1000 W) then stops (power becomes 0). The slope of work-time graph gives instantaneous power. A wrong answer saying both have same power because "both reach 2000 J" ignores the time dimension and the meaning of slope as rate.

questions.q: A student solves: "A 100 W bulb runs for 5 hours. Energy = 100 × 5 = 500 J." Evaluate this solution. Identify the error and give the correct energy in joules and kWh.
questions.a: The solution is incorrect. Error: used power in watts and time in hours directly, giving watt-hours, not joules. Correct: Energy = 100 W × (5 × 3600) s = 1,800,000 J = 1.8 × 10^6 J. In kWh: 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh. A student who accepts 500 J reveals they treat units as labels without dimensional consistency.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household items to compare the power output of two different electric bulbs (e.g., LED vs incandescent) without using a power meter. Describe the procedure, measurements, and calculation.
questions.a: Good answer: Use a calorimeter (or water container) to measure heat energy produced. Immerse each bulb in a known mass of water, run for fixed time, measure temperature rise. Heat energy = mcΔT. Power = energy/time. Compare powers. Poor answer: "Look at brightness" or "check the wattage written on bulb" reveals inability to design a measurement-based experiment and confusion between rated power and actual power.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is ______, measured as work done per unit time.
Fill in the blank: Observe a ceiling fan and a table fan in your classroom: both move air, but the ceiling fan takes ______ to reach full speed.
What is Power? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, measured as work done per unit time.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Power?
questions.a: Students think "higher power means more total energy consumed" and confuse power (rate) with energy (total).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate power from given work and time values with correct SI units, and can explain why two devices doing the same work in different times have different power ratings.
